newsitem.title: CHINA: China tightens control of stock offers abroad.
newsitem.headline: China tightens control of stock offers abroad.

text.p: China tightened controls on Friday on companies offering stock in foreign markets.
China's State Council, or cabinet, said Chinese-controlled companies making share offers abroad must first obtain approval from domestic regulators, state television reported.
It also warned it wanted foreign offers to be made as direct listings, unlike some recent indirect stock sales that had sidestepped Beijing's market regulators.
Firms that ignored the new rules would be punished, it said, though it did not mention specific penalties.
Red chips, Chinese-controlled companies incorporated in Hong Kong, have become the hottest shares on the British colony's stock market.

The initial stock offer by Beijing Enterprises, a red chip company controlled by the Beijing city government, was nearly 1,300 times oversubscribed and its share price tripled on the first day of trading.
The State Council directive did not specifically rule out indirect red chip listings, but it suggested this method of raising cash would be frowned upon in the future.
Much of the excitement over red chips has been generated by expectations of asset injections into the company by the mainland corporate parent after the listing.
The new regulations said provincial- or cabinet-level approval would be needed to transfer assets to a foreign-based company owned by Chinese interests for the purpose of making a stock listing.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission, the country's market watchdog, would then review the proposal and another regulatory body, the Securities Commission of the State Council, would decide on approval.
The directive also repeated a previous ban on the purchase of shell companies to obtain a foreign listing.
Purchases of shell companies were once a popular form of gaining a quick foreign listing, usually in Hong Kong, but this method has been overshadowed by red chip offers in recent years.
